raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining valsartan-mediated angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade with sacubitril-mediated inhibition of neprilysin, thereby augmenting natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin and related vasoactive peptides while suppressing maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system activation [1]. Early human data established blood-pressure reduction and acceptable tolerability, supporting development in heart failure rather than as simple add-on neprilysin inhibition, because unopposed neprilysin inhibition may increase angiotensin II [2].

The pivotal HFrEF programme was designed to test whether ARNI could replace, not merely supplement, ACE inhibition [3]. In PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril/valsartan was superior to enalapril in ambulatory symptomatic HFrEF, reducing the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality and recurrent decompensation, with early and sustained separation of event curves [4]. Subsequent analyses showed fewer episodes of clinical progression among survivors [5] and reductions in both sudden death and pump-failure death [6]. Benefit was broadly consistent across age groups, although hypotension was more common in older patients [7]. Safety analyses suggested slower decline in renal function [8], less severe hyperkalaemia among patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [9], and modestly improved glycaemic control in diabetes [10], while efficacy was maintained in patients with diabetes [11]. Interpretation of natriuretic peptides requires recognition that BNP may rise because it is a neprilysin substrate, whereas NT-proBNP usually falls and retains prognostic value [12,13].

In HFpEF, evidence has been more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and left-atrial reverse remodelling versus valsartan in patients with preserved ejection fraction, providing a biological signal [14]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested heterogeneity, with greater apparent benefit at lower ejection fractions and in women [15,16]. Pooled analyses across ejection-fraction spectra support the concept that ARNI efficacy declines as ejection fraction rises, with the clearest signal in HFrEF and HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction [17]. In patients with recent worsening HF and mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, PARAGLIDE-HF suggested greater NT-proBNP lowering and possible clinical benefit, at the cost of more symptomatic hypotension [18].

Initiation during or soon after hospitalization has become a practical focus. PIONEER-HF demonstrated that, in haemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF, in-hospital initiation produced greater NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia or angioedema [19]. Biomarker analyses showed parallel reductions in myocardial injury and wall-stress markers [20]. TRANSITION supported feasibility of starting sacubitril/valsartan before or shortly after discharge [21], while TITRATION informed up-titration strategies, particularly in patients not previously receiving high-dose ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy [22].

Reverse remodelling data strengthen the biological plausibility of outcome benefits. In PROVE-HF, reductions in NT-proBNP after starting sacubitril/valsartan correlated with improvements in left-ventricular volumes and ejection fraction [23]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant reduction in central aortic stiffness versus enalapril, but did show favourable cardiac structural changes [24]. Conversely, in advanced HFrEF, LIFE found no clear advantage over valsartan and more treatment-limiting intolerance, reminding clinicians that very low blood pressure, frailty and end-stage disease may constrain ARNI use [25]. After acute myocardial infarction complicated by reduced ejection fraction or pulmonary congestion, PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce its primary composite compared with ramipril, although findings were directionally favourable and hypothesis-generating [26].

In contemporary HFrEF care, sacubitril/valsartan is one of four foundational disease-modifying drug classes, alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. DAPA-HF analyses supported compatibility of SGLT2 inhibition with background sacubitril/valsartan [27], and modelling suggests that comprehensive combination therapy can produce large gains in event-free and overall survival [28]. Guidelines therefore recommend ARNI for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, either as replacement for ACE inhibitor/ARB or as first-line renin–angiotensin system inhibition in appropriate patients, with a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors to reduce angioedema risk [29,30]. Practical limitations include hypotension, cost, renal dysfunction during intercurrent illness, hyperkalaemia risk in combination therapy, and underuse or underdosing in real-world practice. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan represents a major advance in HFrEF, a selective option in HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction or lower-range HFpEF, and an exemplar of pathway-based neurohormonal and peptide augmentation therapy.
